hints: Start with the big circle in the centre. Look outside the thin dark lining to the thick wall - what dark-staining supporting tissue do you see in chunks around the wall that also holds the trachea open?

Think about how a bronchus differs from a bronchiole. A bronchus is still a large airway, so it needs support to prevent collapse but also needs to be able to adjust diameter - which tissues allow both?
For the two extra confirming features, compare size and wall structure with the spongy alveoli around it. Look for muscle, overall wall thickness and lumen size.
walkthrough:
Spot the Key Support Tissue**
You are looking at a very large airway lined by ciliated epithelium and surrounded by spongy alveoli. Look in the wall just outside the epithelium for pale-staining blocks of tissue. These are irregular plates of cartilage, not the C-shaped rings of the trachea. Only bronchus (and trachea) have cartilage, bronchioles have none, so this alone identifies bronchus.

Add Supporting Wall Features**
A large airway needs to stay open but also constrict slightly. That is why you also see a layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibres in the wall. The wall is thick and made of many layers, with mucous glands, giving a large round lumen in the centre.

Use Size as a Clue**
Compare the central tube with the tiny air spaces around it. The tube is very large relative to the surrounding alveoli, which fits a bronchus carrying air deep into the lung before branching into smaller bronchioles.

Final answer: Identifying feature: irregular plates of cartilage in the wall. Other confirming features: smooth muscle in wall and large lumen relative to wall thickness / thick multi-layered wall / large size relative to surrounding alveoli.

hints: Look closely at J on the right edge. It is a small tube with a white lumen but it has no ciliated lining and no cartilage. What other tube system runs alongside airways in the lung?
Now compare its wall to its lumen. Is the lumen small and round with a relatively thick muscular wall, or large and irregular with a thin wall? Use that ratio to decide between artery and vein.
walkthrough:
Recognise a Blood Vessel**
J is not an airway because it lacks ciliated epithelium and cartilage and is not a neat round shape like a bronchiole. Its wall shows layers including circular smooth muscle (tunica media), typical of a blood vessel running with the bronchus to supply or drain the lung.

Narrow to Artery**
Look at the proportion of wall to space. J has a very small lumen compared with a thick wall containing much smooth muscle. That thick muscular wall for withstanding higher pressure identifies an artery / arteriole rather than a thin-walled vein.
Final answer: J is an artery (small branch of pulmonary artery). Evidence: small lumen relative to thickness of wall with thick tunica media / thick layer of circular smooth muscle.

hints: Think of the two cell types as a team with two jobs: one makes something sticky, the other has tiny hairs that beat. What would be useful to trap in inhaled air?
Once trapped, where does the dirty material need to go so it does not block the alveoli? Link the beating action to movement toward the throat.
walkthrough:
Trap in Mucus**
Goblet cells in the epithelium produce and secrete a layer of sticky mucus over the lining. Inhaled bacteria, viruses, dust and dirt stick in this mucus instead of reaching the delicate alveoli, which helps prevent infection and damage.

Sweep Away by Cilia**
The ciliated cells have cilia that beat in a coordinated wave. They continuously push / waft the dirty mucus upwards toward the back of the throat where it is swallowed. This mucociliary escalator keeps the lung tissue healthy and clear for gas exchange.
Final answer: Goblet cells secrete mucus to trap pathogens, dust and particles. Cilia beat to waft / move mucus up to the back of the throat to be swallowed, keeping airways clear.
